strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem — orchestration of large, evolving tool ecosystems — and the proposed bilevel decomposition (LLM agent over a four-action decision space + a separately maintained tool dependency graph) is a sensible and clearly articulated design.

The Tool World Navigation Model is well specified: the heterogeneous graph construction (structural + behavioral edges), HGT with statistically weighted attention, hybrid cross-entropy/adaptive-margin training, and the incremental evolution mechanisms (node integration, pruning, edge-weight propagation) are described in enough detail (main text + Appendices A, B) to understand and potentially reimplement.

Evaluation breadth is above average for this line of work: five foundation models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o), two benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank), a real-world RapidAPI test, ablations over every major component (static vs. dynamic graph, Alpha-Beta vs. heuristic search), runtime measurements, and link-prediction quality metrics (Table 8).

Ablations credibly attribute gains to components: the base agent vs. graph-augmented variants (+11.8 TSR on average), dynamic over static graphs on hard tasks, and heuristic over Alpha-Beta search, with consistent trends on both benchmarks and in real-world tests.
Hyperparameters, prompts, training details (Appendix E), and search algorithms (Appendix B.2) are disclosed, supporting reasonable reproducibility of the method itself.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is conducted in a fully simulated environment: API responses, user follow-ups, and success judgments are all produced by LLMs (GPT-4.1 judge, API simulator prompts in E.3.3/E.3.4). This creates a real risk that the simulator rewards fluent, plausible rather than actually correct behavior, and the paper provides no human verification or agreement analysis of the LLM judge. This materially weakens the headline claim of 'best task success rates'.

The claimed closed-loop evolution (contribution iii, Eq. 12, Figure 2 right) is a core motivation ('API drift, continual updates') but is never empirically validated: there is no experiment that injects API failures, deprecations, or new tools and measures recovery/adaptation. The T+1 adaptation in Figure 2 is only illustrative. The 'recent τ days' formulation also has no operational meaning in a static simulated benchmark, suggesting the mechanism is largely untested.

Provenance of the data is under-specified and potentially circular: behavioral chains come from 'historical usage data', but it is unclear what usage logs exist in a synthetic benchmark; task generation (Appendix D) and graph construction appear to derive from the same API lists/trajectories, raising leakage concerns between the trained TWNM and evaluation tasks. The modest link-prediction numbers (AUC 0.71–0.75) are not connected to downstream behavior.

Scalability claims ('scales to thousands of tools') are asserted rather than demonstrated: graphs contain ~7.8k nodes, but there is no analysis of performance or search cost as a function of tool-set size, and runtime tables show the full system (Dynamic+H) is slower than the base agent, partially undercutting the efficiency narrative.

Originality is modest: bilevel decoupling exists in prior multi-stage pipelines (HuggingGPT, α-UMI), and graph-based tool navigation is well explored (ToolNet, ControlLLM, ToolChain*); the contribution is largely a well-executed combination of HGT link prediction, graph search, and prompt-engineered agent scaffolding. The 'first bilevel agent framework' claim is overstated.

Evaluation sets are small (461 ToolBench and 444 API-Bank tasks; only 60 real-world queries against a single baseline), and 'Steps' is counted only for successfully completed tasks, biasing efficiency comparisons; some results show inconsistencies (e.g., GPT-4o Medium TSR drops from 48.9 to a lower value for Dynamic+H vs. Dynamic+A on ToolBench yet Dynamic+H is presented as uniformly best; TCR sometimes lower than α-UMI despite much higher TSR), which are not discussed.

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('tthe', 'an an API', 'TooChain', 'our framework' phrasing), Figure 5 is hard to read, references [37]–[40] are barely integrated into the text, and there is no explicit limitations or reproducibility statement (no code release mentioned).

strengths: The proposed bilevel architecture separating high-level decision making (four-action space) from low-level toolchain execution via a learned tool dependency graph is a coherent and reasonably well-motivated design, and the paper is generally easy to follow.

The evaluation is fairly broad: multiple backbone models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o), two benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank), difficulty-tiered tasks, a supplementary real-world RapidAPI test, and runtime measurements.
The ablation suite (Base vs Static+A vs Dynamic+A vs Dynamic+H) plus link-prediction statistics (Table 8) provides some evidence that graph-based planning contributes beyond the agent itself.
Implementation details (training hyperparameters, prompts, search algorithms) are documented at a level that aids reproducibility of the pipeline mechanics.
weaknesses: Serious circularity risk in the evaluation setup. Tasks are LLM-generated from 'randomful' dependency trees (Appendix D), the API simulator (Appendix E.3.3) returns mock outputs with 'status: success' essentially by construction, and TSR is judged by GPT-4.1 against these same LLM-generated reference chains. The TWNM graph is trained on invocation traces drawn from the same ecosystem, so the model may effectively memorize the very dependency structure from which test tasks were sampled. The paper provides no analysis (e.g., unseen-API or unseen-dependency splits) to rule this out, which undermines the central claims of robustness and generalization.

The headline claims about closed-loop, dynamic adaptation are not empirically validated. Graph evolution (Section 3.2.4, Figure 2) is only illustrated with a stylized example; there is no experiment with API drift, deprecation, or newly introduced tools, despite this being the core motivation ('structured but static' vs 'adaptive but unstructured'). The claim that NaviAgent 'continuously adapts' therefore remains unsupported.

Several reported numbers strain credulity or are internally inconsistent: Deepseek-V3 reaching TCR 97-98% in a simulated environment while Qwen2.5-32B sits near 60%; GPT-4o Dynamic+A Easy TSR (76.4) exceeding the bolded best Dynamic+H (75.3) in Table 2; and baseline TCRs as low as 32% suggesting the evaluation conflates framework quality with prompt/format parsing artifacts. No significance tests or variance estimates are reported for the small test sets (461 ToolBench, 444 API-Bank tasks).

Metric definitions bias the comparison: 'Steps' counts LLM calls only on successfully completed tasks, which disadvantages baselines differently and makes efficiency claims hard to interpret; the runtime table (Table 6) actually shows the proposed Dynamic+H variant is slower than the Base agent on every model, partially contradicting the efficiency framing.

Effectiveness/efficiency gains are sometimes overstated in the text (e.g., 'gains of 12.9, 16.9, 18.7 points' are computed against the average of baselines rather than the strongest baseline alpha-UMI, reducing the margin to ~9-14 points).

The 'first bilevel agent framework' claim is overstated: hierarchical tool classification (Confucius), graph-based search (ControlLLM, ToolChain*, ToolNet), and staged multi-LLM decomposition (alpha-UMI, which also appears to be the 'Base' ablation) already cover closely related ground; the novelty is mostly in combining known components (HGT link prediction, simulated annealing/GA search, alpha-beta pruning) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Technical details contain errors or unexplained choices: the beta-pruning rule prunes when score EXCEEDS the upper bound (S_uv > beta), which is backwards for maximization-style search; the complexity reduction claim to O((sqrt b)^k) from Knuth & Moore is applied to a weighted graph search without justification; many heuristic constants (T0=200, fitness weights 0.35/0.15/0.3/0.15/0.05, eta=0.7) are given without tuning or sensitivity analysis, raising overfitting-to-benchmark concerns.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, the environment, task generator, and evaluator all depend on specific LLMs (GPT-4.1 for judging), and the SFT data is self-generated, so independent verification of results would be very difficult.

Polish is below the bar for a main-track submission: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('tthe strongest', 'an an API is unavailable', 'the our framework', 'This table 4 system displays', 'randomful tree'), a barely legible Figure 5, and formatting inconsistencies (Figures 6/7 are actually algorithms).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: scalable tool orchestration for LLM agents when tool libraries grow to thousands of APIs, and the proposed bilevel decomposition (task-level decision agent vs. execution-level Tool World Navigation Model) is a reasonable and clearly motivated design.

The technical contribution is described in unusual detail: the heterogeneous graph transformer, the hybrid cross-entropy/adaptive-margin link prediction objective, graph evolution mechanisms (incremental node integration, subgraph pruning, edge attribute propagation), and both search algorithms are fully specified in the main text and appendix, including hyperparameters and prompts.

The experimental coverage is broad: five foundation models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o) plus an SFT variant, two benchmarks (ToolBench and API-Bank), three difficulty levels, a real-world RapidAPI test, runtime measurements, and component-wise ablations (Base / Static+A / Dynamic+A / Dynamic+H) that isolate the value of the dynamic graph and the heuristic search, showing consistent TSR gains (e.g., +11.8 points on average from graph-based planning).

Efficiency is treated as a first-class concern: execution steps remain close to the most efficient baseline (ReAct), and runtime is reported honestly, including the admission that the heuristic search increases runtime relative to the Base agent.
Supplementary link-prediction evaluation (Table 8) provides some independent evidence that the graph model itself is learning meaningful tool dependencies.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is conducted in a fully simulated environment: tasks are LLM-generated from dependency trees (Appendix D), API responses are produced by an LLM-based mock simulator, and success (TSR) is judged by GPT-4.1 comparing against a reference path. This creates a circularity risk: the framework's structured JSON-style outputs and its own synthetic task distribution may be systematically favored by both the simulator and the judge. No human evaluation or validation of the LLM judge is provided.

There is no statistical significance testing, variance reporting, or error analysis anywhere; with evaluation sets of only ~460 (ToolBench) and ~444 (API-Bank) tasks, several claimed margins (e.g., 2-3 points between ablation variants) fall within plausible noise ranges.

The 'closed-loop evolution' contribution is asserted but never directly tested: no experiment measures adaptation to API drift, tool addition, or deprecation over time. The graph-evolution behavior is only illustrated qualitatively in Figure 2. Given that adaptivity to evolving ecosystems is the headline motivation, this is a significant evidential gap.

Baselines are limited to ReAct, ToolLLM, and α-UMI. Closely related graph-based and dynamic methods discussed in the related work (ToolNet, ToolChain*, ControlLLM, Confucius) are not compared, weakening claims of state-of-the-art orchestration.

Several claims are overstated: 'the first bilevel agent framework' ignores closely related multi-stage/hierarchical systems (e.g., α-UMI, HuggingGPT, ControlLLM); 'scales to thousands of tools' is supported only indirectly via graph statistics rather than a scalability experiment (e.g., TSR/latency as a function of tool-set size).

The heuristic search is heavily hand-tuned with many magic numbers (fitness weights in Eq. 19, cooling schedules, thresholds α0=0.4, β0=0.9, etc.) with no sensitivity analysis; the modest link-prediction quality (AUC 0.71-0.75) makes the downstream benefit of this elaborate machinery somewhat surprising and under-explained.
The real-world evaluation (Appendix F.1) is small (60 queries, 50 APIs) and only compares against one baseline (α-UMI).

Presentation issues: Figure 5 is effectively unreadable at the rendered size; there are multiple typos ('tthe', 'due to an an API', 'Table 4 system displays', 'the our framework', 'TooChain'); algorithms are labeled 'Figure 6/7' rather than Algorithm floats. No code or data release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the graph construction, task generation, and simulated environment.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank, 50 live RapidAPI endpoints), multiple backbone models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o), and three difficulty levels, with consistent gains in TSR over strong baselines (ToolNet, ToolLLM, Tool-Planner, α-UMI)

Thorough ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each component (bilevel design, graph modeling, static vs. dynamic graph, Alpha-Beta vs. heuristic search, action-level decisions), which strengthens the causal attribution of gains

The system addresses a practically important problem — robustness of tool orchestration to API drift and failure — and the closed-loop graph evolution mechanisms (incremental node integration, targeted pruning with reactivation, edge weight propagation) are concretely specified with maintenance overhead measured in Appendix E.5

The theoretical section (Sec. 3.4, Appendix I) is explicitly and honestly scoped: it claims only a local KL-projection interpretation rather than overstating a global characterization, and the proofs (Theorem I.2, idempotence Proposition, hard-rule corollary) are correct
Reasonable reproducibility support: training hyperparameters, dataset splits, prompts, search algorithm pseudocode, and evaluation rubrics are all provided in the appendix
weaknesses: The core methodology is largely an engineering combination of known components (heterogeneous graph transformer link prediction, alpha-beta pruning, simulated annealing plus genetic algorithms), with many hand-tuned constants (α₀=0.4, β₀=0.9, T₀=200, η=0.7, population 20, fitness weights 0.35/0.15/0.3/0.05/0.05, etc.) and no sensitivity analysis, making the design feel ad hoc and hard to reproduce or transfer

The 'Local Variational View' (Section 3.4) adds little scientific value: the KL projection onto a context-dependent feasible set is a textbook result, and the authors themselves concede it does not model how feasible sets are generated or how the graph evolves; it reads as a decorative formalism appended to an otherwise empirical system

Evaluation quality concerns: main benchmark results rely on simulated environments and LLM-as-judge scoring (GPT-4.1) with no human verification of the judge's reliability, no statistical significance testing or variance across seeds for the reported TSR differences, and the real-world evaluation is small (50 APIs, 303 queries)

Reported gains over the strongest baselines vary substantially by setting and are sometimes modest (e.g., on ToolBench with DeepSeek-V3, Dynamic+H vs. Static+A differences of a few points), and the abstract's headline claims (13.1 point gain, 30% fewer steps) are not consistently reflected in every table

Novelty over closest prior work (ToolNet, which also builds and updates tool graphs from historical interaction) is limited; the main differentiators are the bilevel action space and the recovery mechanisms, whose individual value is shown only in coarse ablations
No mention of code or artifact release, which limits reproducibility of a system with this many implementation-specific heuristics

strengths: The system is evaluated broadly: two standard benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank) across six backbone models of varying scale, plus a real-world experiment on 50 live RapidAPI endpoints covering 303 queries, which is more than many tool-agent papers attempt.

The paper includes reasonably thorough ablations: component-wise ablation (Table 3), TWNM construction variants (Table 4), action-level ablations (Table 11), runtime analysis (Table 7), and a dedicated evaluation of pruning/reactivation under changing API availability (Table 8), which directly tests the 'dynamic ecosystem' claim.

The closed-loop graph maintenance story (incremental node integration, subgraph pruning, edge weight propagation) is concretely specified with equations, and Appendix E.5 quantifies maintenance overhead (e.g., 55 ms node updates, asynchronous retraining), addressing a practical concern.
Appendices provide substantial implementation detail (HGT architecture, search algorithms, prompts, training hyperparameters), which supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies on ToolBench's simulated environment and LLM-judged TSR/TCR, a protocol widely criticized for label noise and bias. No human verification, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical significance testing (no seeds, error bars, or variance) is reported anywhere, so the headline gains (e.g., +8 to +12 TSR) cannot be assessed for reliability.

The theoretical contribution (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.1, Appendix I) is essentially the trivial observation that masking infeasible actions and renormalizing is the KL projection onto the feasible set. The paper itself concedes it is 'intentionally modest' and 'does not fully characterize the TWNM-driven process.' This adds length and an air of rigor without yielding any testable insight or connection to the empirical design.

The method is a loose assembly of many components (bilinear decision agent, HGT link prediction with hybrid CE/margin losses, Alpha-Beta pruning with hand-set thresholds, a simulated-annealing/genetic hybrid search, a composite fitness function Eq. 23 with arbitrary weights 0.35/0.15/0.3/0.15/0.05, path recombination heuristics). No sensitivity analysis for these numerous hyperparameters is provided, raising concerns about overfitting to the benchmark and about generalization; the design appears ad hoc rather than principled.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: graph-structured tool relations with dynamic updates closely resemble ToolNet (Liu et al., 2024b), and planner/executor decoupling, self-verification, and feedback-based adaptation are all established. The paper does not clearly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond recombination.

Real-world validation is thin: only 50 APIs and 303 queries, with no analysis of failure modes, API drift statistics, or cost. The claimed 'robustness under real-world dynamics' is not directly evidenced (Table 8's dynamics experiment is synthetic: randomly designating 10% of APIs as unavailable).

Potential unfairness in comparisons: NaviAgent benefits from task-specific supervised fine-tuning in some settings and bespoke graph machinery, while baselines (ReAct, ToolLLM, ToolNet, etc.) appear to run off-the-shelf with no tuning parity discussion.
Reproducibility is questionable: no code or data release is mentioned despite the system's heavy dependence on many tunable components, prompt templates, and simulation protocol details.

Presentation issues undermine trust: inconsistencies between abstract numbers and tables (e.g., 'average gain of 13.1 points on complex tasks' vs. table deltas), typos such as 'TooChain Retrieval' throughout the case studies, and cluttered figures (Figure 6 is largely unreadable).

strengths: Comprehensive system design combining a bilevel decision agent (four-action decision space) with a graph-based Tool World Navigation Model (TWNM) that captures both structural (schema) and behavioral (invocation-trace) tool dependencies — a reasonable and well-motivated combination for large-scale tool orchestration.

Broad empirical evaluation: results on ToolBench and API-Bank across six backbone models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, plus an SFT variant), ablations of the bilevel design, graph construction, and search strategy (Tables 3, 4, 9, 11), runtime analysis (Table 7), and a dedicated pruning/reactivation experiment under simulated API failures (Table 8).

Real-world validation on 50 live RapidAPI endpoints across 7 domains with 303 queries, showing the simulated-benchmark trends carry over (consistent 4.3–12.0 TSR gains), which partially mitigates concerns about purely simulated evaluation.

Extensive appendix detail (graph construction, HGT architecture, loss functions, search algorithms, prompts, training hyperparameters) and an unusually honest framing of the theoretical contribution in Section 3.4/Appendix I, which explicitly disclaims more than the local KL-projection result actually shows.
SFT results (Figure 5, Table 4) showing a 14B model can approach 32B performance is a practically useful observation about where the gains come from.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is the main concern. TSR is determined by an LLM judge (GPT-4.1) comparing against reference chains in a simulated environment whose API simulator generates mock outputs matching the required format and 'always success' status (Appendix E.3.3). This makes success rates potentially inflated and weakens the central claim; the real-API test (50 APIs, 303 queries) helps but is too small to be decisive. No human evaluation, no inter-rater reliability of the judge, no variance/CI reporting anywhere despite relatively small eval sets (461 ToolBench, 444 API-Bank tasks).

Theorem 3.1 (and its duplicate Theorem I.2) is a textbook KL-projection/renormalization result applied to a hard feasibility constraint; the paper is commendably honest that it is 'deliberately modest,' but as presented it adds little technical content and its connection to the actual TWNM mechanics (how feasible sets arise) is left entirely unspecified.

Numerous hand-tuned heuristics with many magic constants (fitness weights 0.35/0.15/0.3/0.15/0.05, T0=200, η=0.7, P=20, α0=0.4, β0=0.9, pruning threshold 0.7, window size 3, decay 0.9^d, etc.) with essentially no sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about brittleness and whether gains generalize beyond these settings.

Fine-tuning data is generated by the authors' own pipeline (Appendix D) from the same dependency-tree distribution as the evaluation tasks; although train/test splits are stated as disjoint, the shared generative process raises potential distribution-advantage concerns relative to baselines that were not fine-tuned on comparable data.

Carelessness in presentation undermines confidence: Algorithm 1 line 22 uses β ← max(β, 1.15s) while the text specifies β' = min(β, S·1.15); Algorithm 2 ends with 'return G* = 0'; recurring text artifacts such as 'Dynamic+Ally', 'TooChain Retrieval', and the undefined 'D+N(Heur)' notation; Eq. 13's σ(f_freq(v)⁻¹) notation is unclear; Figure 6's caption does not match its content well. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Baseline fairness is not fully addressed: it is unclear whether baselines receive comparable prompt engineering or fine-tuning budgets, and comparisons to ToolNet/ToolPlanner rely on the authors' reimplementation under their own data-generation setup.
No statement about code/data release; given the many dataset-generation prompts and heuristic parameters, reproducibility without artifacts would be difficult.
